There are twenty-nine phrases in the original text:
the first twenty-four phrases separately explain the three types of objects—non-referential (anālambana), phenomena (dharma), and sentient beings (sattva).
Thereafter follow five phrases, which separately explain those sentient beings who take phenomena as objects and those who take nothing as objects.
Of these, the first nine phrases clarify those who take nothing as objects;
the subsequent nine phrases clarify those who take phenomena as objects.
Next, there are six phrases clarifying the objects of sentient beings.
These refer back to the first five [phrases]: because compassion without an object (*anālambana-maitrī*) is free from the grasping of subject and object, one cultivates quiescence (*śānti*);
because it is free from the burning of afflictions (*kleśa*), one cultivates non-maturation (*avipāka*).
Since the principle is uniform across the three periods of time, one cultivates that which is suchness.
Since there is no cause for inequality, one cultivates non-contradiction.
Because there is the arising from the equality of causes, and because all things are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), there are both conformity and contradiction.
Suchness has no cause and is free from contradiction or delusion; therefore, cultivation is non-contradictory.
Suchness has neither interior nor exterior; therefore, cultivation is non-dual.
Sūtra: "Cultivate unbreakable loving-kindness until it is equal to empty space."
The commentary states:
This refers to the compassion without objective conditions (*anālambana-maitrī*), which corresponds to the latter four lines.
Because it is truly and ultimately abiding, its cultivation is indestructible; for there is no time when it is not indestructible.
The old translation says, "Because it is ultimately exhausted. Because all afflictions are ultimately exhausted, its essence is indestructible.

Since the mental disposition of the perceiving subject is like a vajra, the object of observation is as firm and difficult to break; thus, the compassion that is cultivated is called "firm compassion."
Because true nature is fundamentally pure, one cultivates purity.
Because truth is equal to empty space, one cultivates equanimity.
As the Sūtra says: "One cultivates the compassion of an Arhat until it reaches the point of never ceasing."
The commentary states:
The following eleven phrases describe the cultivation of the compassion that takes phenomena as its object (*dharmālambana-maitrī*).
This has three parts:
The first three [verses] concern the three vehicles; the next two, the dharma-guidelines; and the final six, the stages of fruition.
These three sections constitute the "compassion of the three vehicles.
Regarding the compassion of the arhat, there are briefly three meanings:
First, he harms the thieves of afflictions; second, he is free from分段 (fen-duan) birth; third, he is worthy of receiving sublime offerings.
This [verse] takes the first meaning:
because he realizes bodhi alone, he does not depend on a teacher.
Furthermore, it does not depend on material provisions, for it cannot benefit others by means of such provisions;
rather, because the two practices of a bodhisattva benefit sentient beings, they give rise to loving-kindness (*maitrī*) based upon the practices of the two vehicles.
Sūtra: "By cultivating the Tathāgata’s compassion until it reaches all sentient beings.
Commentary:
These two refer to the compassion of the two bodies—the Dharma-body and the Reward-body.

Because True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the principle-dharma of the Dharmakāya Tathāgata, whereas the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is designated as the stage of Buddhahood, there is a distinction between the two.
Sūtra: "Cultivate spontaneous loving-kindness until love and hate are severed."
The commentary states:
This refers to the compassion of the six lower fruit-attainers;
these are the first three lines.
Because the fruition is the spontaneously equal awakening to phenomena, one cultivates spontaneity (*anābhoga*).
Because perfect awakening and suchness are equal in their single flavor, one cultivates bodhi.
Because greed and hatred are eternally extinguished, one cultivates the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Sūtra: Because one cultivates great compassion and loving-kindness up to the contemplation of the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
Commentary:
These are the final three phrases.
One cultivates great compassion in order to manifest the Mahāyāna;
one cultivates non-contention because one contemplates the total absence of self in order to benefit sentient beings,
for if one perceives a self, afflictions will arise.
Because one contemplates the emptiness of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one practices without weariness;
for if the nature of phenomena were existent, there would be weariness.
Sūtra: "One cultivates the compassion of the gift of Dharma until no harm is incurred."
The commentary states:
There are ten phrases below.
Cultivating the object-condition of sentient beings refers to the ten perfections.
Regarding these first three phrases:
"coiling" (juǎn) refers to contracting or drawing back.
It is like a person and an object; at the initial moment the hands are opened, and at a later moment they are drawn together.
The firm dharma is likewise: it begins at first and ceases at the end.
The remaining text is intelligible.
Sūtra: One cultivates the loving-kindness of diligence until one attains direct knowledge of the dharmas.
The commentary states:
This consists of three phrases.
Not being addicted to the flavor of dhyāna is called "being without attachment to flavor."
Constantly accomplishing the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) is called "presently knowing phenomena.
Because it is for the sake of all sentient beings, it is called "compassion conditioned by sentient beings" (*sattvālambanā maitrī*).
As the *Sūtra* states: "By cultivating the compassion of skillful means, one reaches the characteristics of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*)."
The commentary states:
There are four phrases below.
Because they demonstrate skillful means, there is not a single matter that does not bring benefit and happiness; therefore, it is said that "all questions can be universally manifested."
One cultivates the compassion of skillful means because it is brought forth by the ten great vows;
one cultivates the compassion of sublime vows in order to rescue sentient beings;
and one cultivates great power for the sake of simultaneously bringing about their benefit and happiness.
One practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) because one understands the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) in order to awaken sentient beings.
"Na" means wisdom; it refers to the perfection of wisdom. Thus says the Sūtra.
One cultivates the compassion of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) because it reaches all sentient beings.
The commentary states:

The following eight lines separately explain the cultivation of the three types of compassion—those directed toward sentient beings (*sattvālambana*), phenomena (*dharmālambana*), and the objectless (*anālambana*).
The first two concern sentient beings; the next five concern conditioned phenomena (*dharmas*); and the last one concerns the unconditioned (*anālambana*).
These are the objects of sentient beings.
Because it does not destroy the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) while adding the characteristics of dharmas (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) as causes, one cultivates the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Although he manifests various supernatural transformations through his supernormal powers, he does not destroy the nature and characteristics [of phenomena].
This is because, as the *Sūtra* says, he has cultivated non-attached compassion to the point of being free from all defilements.
The commentary states:
These five phrases refer to the objects of focus.
Because the mind is without obstruction and without defilement, one cultivates non-attachment.
Because the mental disposition is pure, it is called being without hypocrisy.
Because the preparatory application is pure, one does not act with guile or crookedness and ensures that every matter is not false; thus, one cultivates non-deception.
Because the mind is free from blemish, one cultivates the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*).
A flaw is a defect of jade.
Although its outward appearance may be fine, if there is impurity within, it is called a flaw and defilement.
The Sūtra says: "Cultivating peaceful and blissful loving-kindness leads to the attainment of peace and bliss."
The commentary states:
This "one objectless" [compassion] is the root of peace and bliss, for it is solely suchness (tathatā).

In the older edition, among the final five phrases clarifying sentient beings, phenomena, and the objectless, one phrase refers to sentient beings, three phrases refer to phenomena, and one phrase refers to the objectless.
Sūtra: From "O Mañjuśrī" up to "cultivating great loving-kindness.
Commentary: This constitutes the *bandha* (concluding seal).
From the passage in the Sūtra where Mañjuśrī speaks up to "cultivating great loving-kindness," the commentary says:
This is the second section.
Sūtra: Vimalakīrti said, “...up to the cultivation of great compassion. Commentary:
This is the second response.

To give without stinginess and to be able to extract sentient beings from the masses of suffering in both the present and the future is called "great compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*), because its practice is vast and extensive.
It is not by mere lack of stinginess that one is named "greatly compassionate," but rather because one bestows happiness upon others.
Sutra: Mañjuśrī spoke, down to "cultivating great goodness.
Commentary:
This is the third question.
The Sūtra says: Vimalakīrti spoke, up to the point of "cultivating great sympathetic joy.
The Commentary says:
This is the third response.
Performing beneficial deeds without regret gives rise to joy;
thus, it is not merely the act of rejoicing in others' merit that is called "joy.
[From the] Sūtra: Mañjuśrī said, up to "cultivating great equanimity."
The commentary states:
This is the fourth question.
In the sutra, Vimalakīrti says, from [the beginning] up to "cultivating great equanimity."
The commentary says:
This is the fourth response.
Herein, equanimity (*upekṣā*) also encompasses impartiality (*samatā*), because there is no hope for recompense.
It is not merely by exhorting the abandonment of evil that one abandons it.
As the Sūtra states, when Mañjuśrī asks, "Ultimately, upon what should one rely?
the commentary says:
The following clarifies the practice for one's own benefit, consisting of twelve successive questions and answers.
This is the first question:
When a bodhisattva prior to the stages enters into birth and death to teach and transform sentient beings, if they experience fear, upon what should they rely?
Because those on the stages do not fear the suffering of birth and death.
The Sūtra says: "Vimalakīrti spoke, reaching up to the 'Great Self' (mahātman) of all Buddhas.
The Commentary states:
This is the answer.
The Great Self of all Buddhas is the Great Nirvana.
The Self of the four virtues is called the Great Self.
Dwelling in non-dwelling is called the correct dwelling of reliance.
The Sūtra further asks: "How does a Bodhisattva dwell within liberation?
The Commentary says:
The second question and answer:

This very *tathatā* (suchness), when free from afflictions (*kleśa*), is conventionally designated as "liberation" (*vimukti*); the essence of liberation is precisely the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The Sūtra further asks: "How is it that one desires to reach the removal of those afflictions?"
The commentary states:
This is the third question and answer.
Its purpose is to eliminate bondage so that the body may attain liberation.
Sūtra: Again he asks about [the stages] from the desire to eliminate up to the attention of observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-manasikāra*).
Commentary:
This is the fourth question and answer.
"Principle" refers to the principles of the two truths and suchness (*tathatā*).
Mental attention that accords with these is called "attention in accordance with principle.
Its essence is the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
Sūtra: He asked again about cultivating the path up to the state of neither-arising-nor-ceasing.
Commentary: This is the fifth question and answer.
Sūtra: It was further asked, "What dharma leads to the non-extinction of the supreme dharmas?
The commentary states:
This is the sixth question and answer.
The abandonment of evil and the cultivation of good is called non-arising and non-ceasing; this correct cultivation arises through reflection.
The Sūtra further asks: "How does goodness reach its culmination? It takes the body as its basis."
The commentary states:
This is the seventh question and answer.
Because there is a body, the wholesome and unwholesome arise.
Because this arises based upon that, it is not the cause that brings about the fundamental [existence].
The Sūtra further asks: "From what does the body arise? It has desire and greed as its basis.
The Commentary says:
The eighth question and answer.

This passage cites the causes for the proximate objects that moisten rebirth as well as craving within the desire realm; therefore, it specifically answers that sensual greed is actually rooted in delusion (*moha*) and so forth.
The Sūtra further asks: "From sensual greed... down to being based on discrimination."
The commentary states:
This is the ninth question and answer.
It is because desire and greed arise from the false discrimination of the grasping mind.
Sūtra: He asked again about the nature of falsehood, [stating that] it is rooted in inverted perceptions (*viparyāsa*). Commentary:
This is the tenth question and answer.
The object of distorted perception exists because a deluded mind arises based on a distorted object.

Therefore, this treatise states: "The disordered appearance and the disordered substance should be admitted as being both material consciousness and non-material consciousness; if one does not exist, the other likewise does not exist."
The old translation says "inverted perception" (*viparyāsa-saṃjñā*); this arises from the mind of discrimination based on the inversion of grasping at mental images.
The Sūtra further asks about inverted perception up to its being rooted in non-abiding.
The commentary states:
This is the eleventh question and answer.
Non-abiding is precisely suchness.
Because, due to delusion regarding suchness, inverted objects arise.
The Sūtra states: "Mañjuśrī spoke... concerning all phenomena.
The Commentary says:
The twelfth question and answer:
True Suchness has no origin, for it is not produced by another.
It is also without grasping or abiding, for it has no further support.

Based on this fundamental ground, all phenomena are established: the nature of defilement arises from delusion, while the nature of purity emerges from awakening. Therefore, the doctrine of Consciousness-Only is taught as the basis for both delusion and awakening; it is called the "establishment of all things," not because it is their producer.
The *Kongliyi* states:
Because non-abiding is itself the nature of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), it is also the fundamental basis for both the two dharmas of delusion and awakening.
Furthermore, since the nature of causes and conditions is empty, all phenomena arise from the nature of emptiness; therefore, it is said that non-abiding establishes all phenomena.
The *Yingliyi* (Principles of Correct Reasoning) states:
If non-Buddhists claim that [the Tathāgata] can produce all things, we reply that our True Suchness (*tathatā*) is not a producer, but rather the basis (*āśraya*) for all phenomena.
Therefore, it is said that "all phenomena are established by relying on nothing," but it is not said that they are produced.
As for what is stated in the sūtras that "the mind creates all," this refers to the mind as cause and condition, not to the mind of dharmatā; therefore, there is no contradiction.
Since dharmatā is not something that can arise, how could it be said to be a creator?
Sūtra: At that time, Vimalakīrti approached the assembly of great śrāvakas and praised them, saying:
"The second section, 'Inferior,' features a celestial maiden who responds to him and refutes the attachments of the śrāvakas."
There are three parts:
first, the celestial maidens scatter flowers; second, the dialogue between Śāriputra and the Buddha; third, Vimalakīrti’s praise.
Within the first part, there are three sections:
First, there is the joyful scattering of flowers; next, the discussion on whether [the auspicious signs] were present or not; and finally, the refutation of attachments through questions and answers.
This is the first section.
Regarding "primordial abiding" (*mūlasthiti*), it clarifies that these signs did not arrive simultaneously with the auspiciousness.
As for the goddess, her rank is that of the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), yet she manifests in the form of a woman.

Therefore, at the end of this chapter, it says: "She is already able to sport with supernatural powers and wisdom, has attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and shall never regress from supreme enlightenment."
"Riding upon the power of her original vow, she accomplishes all that is desired for the sake of all sentient beings.
Thus, we know she is not an ordinary spirit or ghost.

Furthermore, because women generally possess deep compassion and a profound sense of pity, they are able to benefit those in the dark realms through skillful means; how much more so when she seeks to transform the śrāvakas, leading them away from defiled attachments by manifesting the act of scattering flowers, thereby assisting in the promotion of stainless capability. For this reason, she assumes a female body rather than a male form.
Since it is a manifested form (*nirmāṇa-rūpa*), it is not fixed as belonging to any particular heaven.
Based on its superior majesty and beauty, it most likely belongs to the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*).
This is why, in the past, Vimalakīrti used his "empty room" to conceal his physical form.
Now, for the sake of benefit and expediency, his body has manifested.

As for those who scattered flowers—flowers that were abundant, fragrant, and exquisite—it was because the ignorant and worldly are stained by emotional attachments; to clarify that while the Śrāvakas possess such attachments, the Bodhisattvas remain free from them, they thus scattered them.

Furthermore, flowers conceal foul odors and encounter fragrances; they possess the capacity for immediate blooming and flourishing, and the virtue of eventually bearing fruit. For these reasons, one scatters only flowers and not other things.
On the fifteenth day of the fifth month of the Cultural Dingsou year, I finished collating this scroll. This scroll contains particularly many transcription errors.
Regarding those points difficult to verify and correct, I have either retained the original text;
furthermore, even where I have made corrections, I did not presume to decide them on my own authority.

Within this work, however, across the two sheets comprising fascicles three and four, the explanations of subject and object are intermingled and difficult to disentangle; though I have been subjected to criticism and met with derision, I have disregarded such mockery to provide supplementary guidance for the ignorant, interpreting the sutras according to my own private views and arranging them in sequential order.
May future sages not merely take this as a model for emulation.
With profound reverence and without confusion, I have transcribed the nine-fascicle edition of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*.
